title: Maths-for-ML bridge
summary: Connect the maths you already know to the four pillars machine learning actually uses: vectors, matrices, derivatives, and probability.
objectives: Represent data as vectors and matrices with NumPy
Compute dot products and understand them as similarity and weighted sums
Use matrix multiplication to apply a model to many rows at once
Explain gradients and how gradient descent minimises a loss
Read probability notation and apply Bayes' rule to a simple problem
Recognise the four maths pillars inside a real ML training loop

quiz.q: What does the dot product of two vectors give you?
quiz.why: The dot product sums the element-wise products, producing one scalar — a weighted sum used everywhere in ML.

quiz.q: In gradient descent, which direction do you step to reduce the loss?
quiz.why: The gradient points uphill (steepest increase), so we step in the negative gradient direction to go downhill toward a minimum.

quiz.q: For NumPy arrays A (shape 3x2) and B (shape 2x4), what is the shape of A @ B?
quiz.why: Matrix multiplication requires inner dimensions to match (2 and 2); the result takes the outer dimensions, giving 3x4.

quiz.q: What is a gradient, in one sentence?
quiz.answer: The vector of partial derivatives of a function — it points in the direction of steepest increase.
quiz.why: Each component is the slope with respect to one variable; together they say which way the function rises fastest.

quiz.q: State Bayes' rule and what it lets you do.
quiz.answer: P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B); it flips a conditional probability so you can update a belief given new evidence.
quiz.why: It is the backbone of probabilistic ML — turning P(evidence|cause) into P(cause|evidence).

quiz.q: Why do we use matrices instead of looping over rows one at a time?
options: Vectorised matrix maths is far faster and clearer
Loops are not allowed in Python
quiz.why: Libraries like NumPy run matrix operations in fast compiled code, processing every row at once — vectorisation beats Python loops for speed and readability.

body_markdown:
## Why this lesson?

You already have the hard part — a maths degree. The goal here is **translation**, not new theory: matching the four pieces of maths that machine learning leans on to the language ML practitioners use. Those four pillars are **vectors**, **matrices**, **derivatives (gradients)**, and **probability**.

We'll do all of it in code with NumPy, because in ML you rarely compute by hand — you describe the maths and let the library run it fast.

## Vectors: data as arrows

A **vector** is just an ordered list of numbers. One data point — say a house with size, bedrooms, and age — becomes a vector `[120, 3, 10]`. The **dot product** multiplies matching entries and sums them into a single number.

```python
import numpy as np

x = np.array([120, 3, 10])      # features
w = np.array([0.5, 20, -1.0])   # weights
prediction = x @ w              # dot product -> scalar
print(prediction)               # 110.0
```

That dot product is a **weighted sum** — the core operation inside almost every model. It also measures similarity: aligned vectors give a large value.

## Matrices: many rows at once

Stack many data vectors as rows and you get a **matrix**. **Matrix multiplication** applies the same weights to every row in one go — this is *vectorisation*, and it is far faster than a Python loop.

```python
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[120, 3, 10],     # 3 houses
              [80,  2, 25],
              [150, 4, 2]])
w = np.array([0.5, 20, -1.0])
predictions = X @ w             # one prediction per row
print(predictions)              # [110.  70. 133.]
```

Remember the shape rule: `(m x n) @ (n x p) = (m x p)`. The inner dimensions must match.

## Derivatives: how models learn

Training means **minimising a loss** — a number measuring how wrong the model is. The **gradient** is the vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each weight; it points uphill. So we step the *other* way. That loop is **gradient descent**:

```python
w = w - learning_rate * gradient
```

Repeat thousands of times and the weights settle where the loss is small. Every "learning" algorithm you'll meet is some flavour of this idea.

## Probability: reasoning under uncertainty

ML outputs are rarely certain — they're **probabilities**. You'll read `P(A|B)` as "probability of A given B". The key tool is **Bayes' rule**, which flips a conditional so you can update a belief when new evidence arrives:

`P(A|B) = P(B|A) * P(A) / P(B)`

This underpins spam filters, classifiers, and anything that reasons from evidence to cause.

## Your task

Using NumPy, build a 4x3 feature matrix and a length-3 weight vector, then compute all four predictions with a single `@`. Confirm by hand that one row matches.

slides.narration: Welcome back. You arrived on this course with a maths degree, which means the hardest part is already behind you. In this lesson we're not learning new theory. We're translating the maths you already know into the four pillars that machine learning actually uses: vectors, matrices, derivatives, and probability. By the end you'll recognise all four inside a real training loop.

slides.title: The four pillars
bullets: Vectors — single data points as lists of numbers.
Matrices — many data points stacked together.
Gradients — how a model learns from error.
Probability — reasoning when answers aren't certain.
slides.narration: Here's the whole map. Machine learning leans on four pieces of maths. Vectors represent a single data point. Matrices stack many points together so we can process them at once. Gradients tell a model how to improve from its mistakes. And probability lets us reason when answers aren't black and white. Everything else is built on these four.

slides.title: Vectors: data as numbers
bullets: A vector is an ordered list of numbers.
One data point becomes one vector.
In code, a NumPy array.
slides.code:
import numpy as np

x = np.array([120, 3, 10])
print(x.shape)   # (3,)
slides.narration: Let's start with vectors. A vector is simply an ordered list of numbers. Picture a house described by its size, its number of bedrooms, and its age. That becomes the vector one-twenty, three, ten. In code we use a NumPy array, and its shape tells us it holds three values. Nothing mysterious — just data lined up.

slides.title: The dot product
bullets: Multiply matching entries, then sum.
Result is a single number, a scalar.
It's a weighted sum — the heart of a model.
slides.narration: Now the single most important operation: the dot product. You multiply matching entries and add them up, giving one number. Here our features meet a set of weights and produce one-hundred and ten. That's a weighted sum, and it sits at the heart of almost every model. The at symbol in NumPy computes it for us.

slides.title: Matrices: many rows
bullets: Stack data vectors as rows of a matrix.
Each row is one example.
Shape tells you rows by columns.
slides.narration: Real datasets have thousands of examples, not one. So we stack the vectors as rows, and that gives us a matrix. Here three houses become a three-by-three matrix: three rows, one per house, and three columns, one per feature. The shape attribute always tells you rows by columns, which you'll check constantly.

slides.title: Matrix multiplication
bullets: Apply weights to every row in one step.
This is vectorisation — fast and clean.
Shape rule: inner dimensions must match.
slides.narration: Here's the payoff. Instead of looping over each house, matrix multiplication applies the weights to every row at once. We call this vectorisation, and it's both faster and cleaner than a Python loop. Just watch the shape rule: an m-by-n matrix times an n-by-p matrix needs those inner n's to match. Get one prediction per row, instantly.

slides.title: Derivatives & loss
bullets: Loss measures how wrong the model is.
The gradient points uphill on that loss.
It's the vector of partial derivatives.
slides.narration: Now, how does a model actually learn? First we define a loss: a single number measuring how wrong our predictions are. Then we use the gradient. The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each weight, and it points in the direction the loss increases fastest. In other words, it points uphill, toward worse.

slides.title: Gradient descent
bullets: Step opposite the gradient to go downhill.
Repeat until the loss stops shrinking.
Every learning algorithm is a flavour of this.
slides.narration: If the gradient points uphill, then to reduce our error we step the other way — opposite the gradient, downhill. That's this one line: new weights equal old weights minus a small learning rate times the gradient. Repeat it thousands of times and the weights settle where the loss is small. Almost every learning algorithm you'll meet is a flavour of this idea.

slides.title: Probability & Bayes
bullets: ML outputs are often probabilities, not certainties.
Read P(A given B) as a conditional probability.
Bayes' rule flips it to update a belief.
slides.narration: Our last pillar is probability. Machine learning rarely gives a flat yes or no — it gives a probability. You'll read P of A given B as the probability of A when B is true. The key tool is Bayes' rule, which flips that conditional around. It lets you update a belief as new evidence arrives, and it powers spam filters and classifiers everywhere.

slides.title: The four pillars in one loop
bullets: Vectors and matrices hold the data.
Dot products produce predictions.
Gradients update the weights each step.
Probabilities express the final output.
slides.narration: Let's see them together. In a real training loop, vectors and matrices hold your data. Dot products turn that data into predictions. Gradients nudge the weights a little better on every step. And probabilities express how confident the final answer is. Four pillars, one loop. Once you spot this pattern, every model starts to look familiar.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Vector = a data point; dot product = weighted sum.
Matrix = many rows; multiply to predict all at once.
Gradient descent steps downhill to cut the loss.
Bayes' rule updates beliefs from evidence.
Task: build a 4x3 matrix and predict with one @.
slides.narration: Let's recap the bridge. A vector is one data point, and the dot product turns it into a weighted sum. A matrix stacks many rows, and matrix multiplication predicts them all at once. Gradient descent steps downhill to shrink the loss. And Bayes' rule updates our beliefs from evidence. Your task before next time: build a four-by-three feature matrix and a weight vector, then compute all four predictions with a single at symbol. Check one row by hand. See you next lesson.
